patient.chief_complaint: Recurring 15-20 minute episodes of word-finding difficulty — third episode, GP concerned about TIA
patient.hpi:
A 52-year-old British woman was urgently referred to the neurology outpatient clinic after three episodes over the past 4 months of transient expressive language difficulty. Each episode has a similar character: she suddenly becomes unable to find words she knows, using substituted or circumlocutory language ('the thing you use to write with' instead of 'pen'), and those around her notice she is speaking in broken, effortful phrases. She remains fully conscious and aware during the episode and is frustrated by her inability to express herself. The episodes develop gradually over approximately 5-8 minutes, peak in severity around 10-15 minutes, then resolve over another 5-8 minutes — total duration 15-25 minutes. Each episode has been followed within 10-30 minutes by a left-sided throbbing headache, photophobia, and nausea rated 7/10 lasting 8-12 hours.

Her GP immediately referred her for urgent TIA assessment given the language symptoms and her age. She has mildly elevated cholesterol (on atorvastatin 20 mg started after the first episode by her GP). She has no hypertension, no AF, no diabetes, and no prior stroke. She is a non-smoker. She is post-menopausal (stopped periods age 51). She is not on any hormonal therapy. Her husband has severe migraines with visual aura. She has no prior personal history of migraine. On very careful questioning during the neurology consultation, she recalls that approximately 5-10 years ago she occasionally had brief episodes of 'colours in her vision' for a few minutes that she dismissed — she never told anyone.

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing post-menopausal woman; alert and fully oriented; articulate and fluent today; no speech difficulty between episodes
physical_exam.neurological: Normal language function: fluent speech, normal repetition, normal comprehension, normal naming (including confrontation naming of objects). Normal cranial nerves II-XII. ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with aphasic aura (G43.1); three episodes; TIA excluded by normal DWI, MRA, cardiac workup; late-onset de novo aura in postmenopausal woman

differential.key_features: Normal DWI on MRI; normal carotid MRA; no AF on 48-hour Holter; normal echocardiogram; no cardioembolic source; gradual onset over 5-8 min (TIA = abrupt); consistent subsequent headache in all 3 episodes; prior brief visual episodes confirm longstanding migraine predisposition
differential.distinguishing_test: Brain MRI DWI (normal); MRA (no left MCA stenosis); Holter (no AF); echo (no PFO)

differential.diagnosis: Focal seizure with ictal aphasia (left temporal)
differential.key_features: Ictal aphasia from left temporal focus typically has brief, stereotyped, sub-minute onset; duration 5-8 min for onset is too gradual for seizure propagation; EEG no left temporal epileptiform activity; followed by migrainous headache not post-ictal state
differential.distinguishing_test: EEG (no left temporal epileptiform discharges; non-specific left temporal-parietal slowing only)

differential.key_features: Episodes are fully reversible within 25 minutes — primary progressive aphasia causes progressive deterioration; fully fluent and normal naming between episodes; only 4-month history
differential.distinguishing_test: Clinical assessment (complete reversibility); MRI (no cortical atrophy or signal change)

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with DWI and MRA (intracranial + carotid) — exclude left hemisphere TIA and carotid disease
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal DWI; no left perisylvian infarct; normal MCA and carotid MRA

optimal_actions.action: Prolonged cardiac monitoring (≥48 hours Holter) — AF exclusion is critical for aphasic TIA vs migraine
Echocardiogram — exclude cardioembolic source (LA thrombus, PFO, valvular disease)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal; no PFO; no LA thrombus; normal valves

optimal_actions.action: Discontinue aspirin — diagnosis is migraine with aphasic aura, not TIA; aspirin not indicated
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Aspirin empirically started for suspected TIA; diagnosis confirmed as migraine; discontinue

optimal_actions.action: Initiate topiramate preventive therapy (25 mg titrating to 50-100 mg)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: 3 disabling aphasic aura episodes in 4 months = preventive therapy clearly indicated

critical_actions: Recognise gradual 5-8 minute onset of aphasia = characteristic of CSD spread, not TIA (which is abrupt onset)
Full TIA workup is warranted given clinical uncertainty — all negative, confirming migraine diagnosis
Identify prior brief visual episodes from 5-10 years ago as early incomplete visual aura — confirms longstanding migraine predisposition pre-dating current aphasic episodes
Discontinue aspirin — prescribed empirically for TIA but diagnosis is now confirmed as migraine with aura
Late-onset de novo migraine aura in postmenopausal women is a recognised entity — oestrogen decline alters CSD threshold
contraindicated_actions: Do not anticoagulate for assumed TIA without confirmed DWI restriction or embolic source
Do not continue aspirin — diagnosis is migraine with aphasic aura; aspirin is not primary CV prevention in 2024 guidelines at this risk level
Do not diagnose primary progressive aphasia — episodes are fully reversible
key_reasoning_points: The gradual onset (5-8 minutes) of expressive aphasia is the CRITICAL feature distinguishing aphasic migraine aura from TIA — TIA produces abrupt maximal-onset aphasia
Each aphasic episode followed within 30 minutes by a migrainous headache is highly characteristic — TIA is not followed by migrainous headache in most cases
Late-onset de novo migraine aura in postmenopausal women is increasingly recognised — oestrogen decline alters CSD susceptibility
Prior brief visual episodes 5-10 years ago represent early incomplete visual aura — this woman had migraine predisposition long before overt aphasic aura episodes
Puzzle difficulty: aphasia at age 52 with vascular risk factors in a post-menopausal woman strongly suggests TIA to most initial assessors; complete workup is negative

output.query: migraine aphasic aura ICHD-3 TIA differentiation gradual onset late onset postmenopausal

results.finding: ICHD-3 migraine with aphasic aura: language symptoms (expressive aphasia, word-finding difficulty, paraphasias) as the aura — develops gradually over ≥5 min, lasts 5-60 min, followed by headache within 60 min. Gradual onset over 5-8 minutes with subsequent headache is the KEY differentiating feature from TIA (abrupt onset, no subsequent headache). TIA produces sudden-onset aphasia, usually with receptive or global component. Migraine with aura can present de novo in peri/post-menopausal women — oestrogen decline alters CSD threshold. Prior brief visual episodes ('colours in vision') 5-10 years ago likely represent early incomplete visual aura.

output.summary: ICHD-3 migraine with aphasic aura: language symptoms developing gradually over 5 minutes or more, lasting 5-60 minutes, followed by headache within 60 minutes. Abrupt-onset aphasia is characteristic of TIA; gradual onset with subsequent headache is characteristic of migraine aura. Prior brief visual episodes may represent incomplete visual aura in individuals with migraine predisposition.

output.query: aspirin migraine with aura TIA prevention postmenopausal primary prevention 2024

results.source: NICE guidelines; AHA/ASA secondary prevention guidelines
results.finding: Aspirin is indicated for secondary prevention after confirmed TIA or ischaemic stroke. There is no evidence that aspirin reduces migraine aura frequency or headache episodes; it is not recommended as a migraine-specific preventive. Current guidelines do not support aspirin for primary cardiovascular prevention in the absence of confirmed vascular events, given a neutral to negative risk-benefit balance. Statin therapy is appropriate for hypercholesterolaemia; lifestyle modification for borderline vascular risk factors is consistent with current guidance.

output.summary: Aspirin is indicated only for confirmed secondary prevention after TIA or stroke; it is not a recommended migraine preventive; current guidelines do not support aspirin for primary CV prevention in this risk profile. Statin therapy is recommended for hypercholesterolaemia.

output.query: migraine prevention postmenopausal woman topiramate amitriptyline atorvastatin interactions

results.source: AAN/EAN migraine prevention guidelines; geriatric neurology review
results.finding: Recurrent disabling migraine with aura at a frequency of ≥4 attacks per month is a recognised indication for preventive therapy. Topiramate 25-100 mg/day — Level A evidence for migraine prevention; no clinically significant interaction with atorvastatin; monitor serum bicarbonate. Amitriptyline 10-50 mg QHS — Level B; QTc monitoring is prudent in older patients. Valproate is generally avoided in older women due to association with cognitive decline. Anti-CGRP antibodies are an option after first-line agent failure; no interactions with statins.

output.summary: Topiramate preferred preventive (Level A; weight-neutral/beneficial; no statin interaction); amitriptyline alternative; avoid valproate in older women
